entries.human_title: Ampharos H1 — Aquapolis opens the holo city with a signal

special_identification_instructions.summary: Identify Ampharos H1 by the Aquapolis H-number Rare Holo lane: English ecard2-H1 / H1/H32, not the non-Holo #1 row and not the Japanese E3-049 row.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Aquapolis Ampharos, Ampharos H1, H1/H32, Rare Holo, ecard2-H1, Shin-ichi Yoshida, Thundershock, Reflect Energy, Wind from the Sea, E3-049, Aquapolis #1, Expedition Ampharos, Neo Ampharos, or reverse holo Ampharos.

entries.why_it_matters: Aquapolis could have opened its holo lane with a dragon or a legend. Instead H1 is Ampharos: Johto's lighthouse Pokemon, quiet and useful, standing at the edge of a set built like a coastal machine. The charm is exactly there. Shin-ichi Yoshida's Ampharos is not the loudest chase in Aquapolis, but it is the right first light for a set where cardboard, data, water, and electricity all start talking to each other.

entries.human_title: Exeggutor H10 — Aquapolis lets the heads gamble

special_identification_instructions.summary: Identify Exeggutor / ナッシー / Nassy H10 by the Aquapolis H-number Rare Holo lane: English ecard2-H10 / H10/H32 and Wind from the Sea 014/087 lineage, not the non-Holo #12 / 013/087 row.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Aquapolis Exeggutor, ナッシー, Nassy, Exeggutor H10, H10/H32, Rare Holo, ecard2-H10, Yukiko Baba, Super Eggsplosion, Called Shot, Wind from the Sea, 014/087, Aquapolis #12, Jungle Exeggutor, or reverse holo Exeggutor.

entries.why_it_matters: Exeggutor H10 is not one of the obvious Aquapolis monsters, and that is part of the fun. It makes the set feel inhabited: a strange Grass holo in a coastal machine, drawn by Yukiko Baba, asking you to throw Energy away and count heads like the card itself is laughing. The agent's job is to keep that charm pinned to the exact H10 holo object, because the non-holo #12 is nearby and dangerously easy to blur.

entries.human_title: Houndoom H11 — the dark dog with two shadows

special_identification_instructions.summary: Identify Houndoom / ヘルガー / Hellgar H11 by the Aquapolis H-number Rare Holo lane: English ecard2-H11 / H11/H32 and The Town on No Map 071/092 lineage, not the non-Holo #15 / 070/092 sibling or the Fire-type #14 / 019/092 false friend.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Aquapolis Houndoom, ヘルガー, Hellgar, Houndoom H11, H11/H32, Rare Holo, ecard2-H11, Hajime Kusajima, Fireworks, Dark Impact, C-75, C-75-#, The Town on No Map, 071/092, Aquapolis #15, Aquapolis #14, Naoyo Kimura, Smokescreen, Burn Up, or reverse holo Houndoom.

entries.why_it_matters: Houndoom H11 is exactly why this catalog needs identification instructions. It looks clean at first: Aquapolis, H-number holo, Hajime Kusajima, Darkness type. Then the set folds back on itself. There is a non-holo #15 that shares the same artist and attack text, and a separate #14 Houndoom that belongs to a different Fire-type route. The pleasure is in the precision: the agent has to hold the card's menace and its paperwork at the same time.

entries.why_it_matters: Hypno H12 is a perfect Aquapolis card because the old character gimmick becomes machinery. The pendulum is not just flavor; it is Sleep Pendulum, then Spiral Aura, then an e-Reader strip with Dream Eater waiting behind it. Mitsuhiro Arita gives the card the old TCG gravity, but the H12 identity still has to be held carefully, because the non-holo #16 is almost a mirror.

entries.why_it_matters: Jumpluff H13 is a lovely test of what this catalog is trying to do. The card feels light: Yuka Morii, fluff, cotton, a Pokemon that rides the wind. But the identification work is not light at all. The agent has to hold H13 as the holo object, #17 as the non-holo sibling, and the C-63 e-Reader strip as a tiny doorway into Construction: Action without pretending any of it proves the seller's card.

entries.why_it_matters: Base Set 2 Clefable is gentle until you read it. Arita draws the soft fairy shape, but Metronome gives it a mischievous old-TCG power: it can borrow the enemy's own attack without becoming the enemy. Minimize then turns the card into a small moonlit dodge. That is why Clefable matters in this catalog. It is not a Charizard-style roar; it is Pokemon learning that cute can be strange, tactical, and a little theatrical. Base Set 2 preserves that Jungle feeling inside a reprint set, which makes the protocol lesson just as important as the collector one: the same fairy, same artist memory, and same attack text can still belong to different physical lanes. The symbol and number have to speak before the agent spends.

entries.why_it_matters: Base Set 2 Magneton is early Pokemon at its most wonderfully mechanical. It is not a dragon, not a mascot, not a mythic creature. It is three Magnemite becoming a problem together. Kinebuchi's object-like rendering gives the holo a different charge from the soft character cards around it: metal, pull, surface, glare. Thunder Wave promises paralysis; Selfdestruct promises that power has a bill, splashing damage across both Benches and back onto Magneton itself. That is why the card is good catalog training. The same species threads through Base Set, Japanese No Rarity PMCG1-039, Fossil, Dark Magneton, Lt. Surge's ownership grammar, Quick Starter, and later reprints. The agent can love the strange machine, but the symbol, number, and evidence still decide which machine is actually in hand.

entries.human_title: Alakazam #1 — the mind in the scanner

special_identification_instructions.summary: Expedition Alakazam #1 is a finish-and-interface trap: the famous name is not enough; the agent must preserve set, number, finish, B-84/B-84-#, Box Topper, and test-print boundaries.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Expedition Alakazam, Alakazam #1, ecard1-1, Hajime Kusajima, Psymimic, Syncroblast, B-84, B-84-#, Box Topper, reverse holo, test card, For Position Only, Base Set, Base Set 2, Legendary Collection, or Dark Alakazam.

entries.why_it_matters: Expedition Alakazam #1 feels like a thesis card for the e-Reader era. It is still Alakazam, still the old psychic fantasy of calculation and control, but the old Damage Swap memory has been rebuilt as Psymimic: copy the opponent, pay the cost, make the other side's move pass through your own machine. Then the border starts talking too. B-84, B-84-#, Box Topper, test print, short strip, no long strip, Crystal Pokedex text, Kusajima watercolor and ink. The card is not just a holo at the front of a set; it is Pokemon learning to make a printed object behave like an interface.

entries.why_it_matters: Expedition Dugtrio #10 is wonderful because it is humble and dangerous at the same time. It is not a mascot, not a legendary, not the front-window chase. It is three heads in the dirt carrying one of Pokemon's oldest physical ideas: the ground moves underneath everything. Magnitude hits both Benches, the Crystal Pokedex text talks about earthquakes sixty miles down, and the e-Reader frame gives that underground force an A-17 machine address. The agent lesson is perfect: this is not just Dugtrio, and not even just Expedition Dugtrio. It is #10 Rare Holo, beside #44 non-holo, with the same artist and attacks but a different evidence lane.

Kusajima's first English cards arrive in Expedition, so this Johto final evolution also marks an artist entering English binders through the e-Reader door. The card feels like a greenhouse wired to a machine: petals, healing, poison, B-66, and a fat border waiting for hardware. And the catalog work matters because Meganium is especially easy to blur. #18 and #54 share the same body of rules; #53 is a different Meganium; reverse holo is its own lane; Neo Genesis is a different memory. The flower calms the room, but the assembly keeps the room honest.

special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing or want references Dark Espeon, Espeon, Eeveelution, or Neo Destiny number 4.

entries.why_it_matters: Dark Espeon has the strange pull of an almost-complete thought. The set darkens several Eevee branches, but not Umbreon, so Espeon ends up carrying extra atmosphere: elegant, psychic, and just off-center. Atsuko Nishida's credit makes that turn feel even more intimate, because the card asks a soft creature to wear the set's shadow.

entries.why_it_matters: This Espeon has that early-Johto thrill: Eevee suddenly has a future that feels graceful instead of simply stronger. In Neo Discovery, the holo slot makes that branching feel ceremonial. Atsuko Nishida's credit gives the card an origin-touch too; one of Pokemon's defining designers is there when the Eeveelution family opens another door.

entries.why_it_matters: Tyranitar is the moment Neo Discovery stops whispering and starts rumbling. The ruins mood is still there, but this card turns it into mass: a Darkness-type final evolution with an attack literally called Trample. Hironobu Yoshida's row feels like Johto's mystery developing teeth.

special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, or binder import says Neo Revelation Lugia, Neo Lugia, Aerowing, or Lugia 20/64.

entries.why_it_matters: Lugia 20 is not the thunderclap Lugia from Neo Genesis, and that is the point. entries.why_it_matters: Shining Gyarados is where Neo Revelation earns its name. A familiar monster returns as an impossible color and even the numbering admits the card sits past the printed wall. entries.why_it_matters: Shining Magikarp is perfect Pokemon mischief. For an agent, this card teaches a beautiful lesson: sometimes the chase is not scarcity alone, but format, mail route, account credit, artist signature, and the evidence of a club talking back to its members.

entries.human_title: The city where the card became an interface

special_identification_instructions.summary: Aquapolis identity depends on e-Reader strips, H-number holos, secret rows, and count-basis conventions; agents should keep those boundaries visible.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: Identifying or comparing Aquapolis cards, especially H-number holos, Crystal Pokemon, or secret-number rows.

entries.why_it_matters: Aquapolis feels like Wizards building a coastal machine out of cardboard. The Pokemon are still there, but the frame has become stranger: H numbers, Dot-Code strips, hidden data, Crystal Type, and secret rows. It is beautiful because it is slightly overbuilt. A collector is not only holding a picture; they are holding the remains of a moment when the card wanted to talk to hardware.

entries.human_title: The doorway most collectors learned first

special_identification_instructions.summary: English Base Set is the 102-row English launch expansion modeled as base1. Preserve set id, row number, language, and edition/Shadowless evidence before comparing it to Japanese launch cards or later reprints.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Base Set, base1, English Base, original English Pokemon cards, Shadowless, First Edition, Unlimited, no expansion symbol, or same art as Japanese Expansion Pack.

entries.why_it_matters: English Base is where a huge part of the English-speaking world learned the shape of Pokemon cards: the Charizard gravity, the starter trio, the trainers that taught the game, the energy floor, the Ken Sugimori and Mitsuhiro Arita visual grammar. In this catalog it is useful, beloved, and dangerous. It helps an agent explain why an older Japanese row feels familiar, but it must never let familiarity become provenance. English Base is a doorway, not a shortcut.

special_identification_instructions.summary: Base Set 2 is a 130-row English reprint/compilation release. Preserve set id base4, row number, and Base Set 2 symbol before comparing to Base Set, Jungle, Shadowless, or First Edition copies.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Base Set 2, base4, Charizard, Blastoise, Venusaur, Base Set art, Jungle art, Shadowless, First Edition, or same artwork.

entries.why_it_matters: Base Set 2 is strange in a useful way. It is not the first spark, and it is not trying to be. It is the early English game learning to package its own memory: Base Set icons, Jungle favorites, familiar trainer tools, and the energy floor gathered into a new object with a new symbol. For a collector, that can feel less pure than a first print. For an agent, it is a perfect lesson: resemblance is not provenance. Same art, different assembly.

entries.human_title: The prize table at the edge of Wizards

special_identification_instructions.summary: Best of Game is a nine-row English promo series under set id bp. Preserve row id, Winner-stamp status, jumbo status, and source release before comparing to Gym Challenge or other branches.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Best of Game, bp, Winner stamp, Rocket's Mewtwo, Rocket's Scizor, Rocket's Sneasel, Dark Venusaur, jumbo, BattleZone, or Gym Challenge.

entries.why_it_matters: Best of Game feels like a little end-of-era packet. It is only nine rows, but it carries a lot of machinery: Winner stamps, Rocket ownership, Dark evolution, jumbo echoes, and the feeling of cards moving through tournaments rather than booster packs. The set is not trying to be a world. It is a receipt from organized play, with just enough villain shine to make the receipt collectible.

entries.human_title: The promo star as a map of first contact

special_identification_instructions.summary: The Black Star family is a distribution network. Agents should identify the specific row and route before using promo history as trust or value context.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: Explaining or comparing Wizards Black Star Promo cards.

entries.why_it_matters: Wizards Black Star Promos are not a normal set pretending to be a checklist. They are the trail of early English Pokémon meeting people in public: league tables, movie lines, guidebooks, mail-in activities, a New York store opening, home video, magazines. The cards feel scattered because they are scattered; that is the point. Their assembly history is the story.

entries.human_title: When the border became a machine

special_identification_instructions.summary: Expedition identification is row plus interface: the e-Reader border is part of the card's identity, but catalog data does not prove a seller's strip is readable.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: Identifying Expedition Base Set cards or comparing holo/non-holo e-Card rows.

entries.why_it_matters: Expedition is a beautiful hinge. The old Wizards chase language is still there: Charizard, Blastoise, Mew, Tyranitar, Venusaur. But the card frame has changed its job. The fat left and bottom borders are not just design; they are an attempt to make cardboard speak to hardware. For a catalog about assembly, Expedition is where the object admits it wants to be read by more than human eyes.

special_identification_instructions.summary: English Fossil is a 62-row Wizards release; preserve language, set id, row number, and holo/non-holo distinction.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Fossil, English Fossil, Mystery of the Fossils, legendary birds, Fossil Dragonite, Fossil Gengar, or Mysterious Fossil.

entries.why_it_matters: Fossil is one of those early sets that changes the room temperature. Jungle made the world feel alive; Fossil makes it feel buried, haunted, and waiting to be uncovered. The legendary birds give the sky a mythic ceiling, Gengar gives the caves a grin, Dragonite gives the set a soft surprise, and Mysterious Fossil makes the idea of recovery mechanical. It is not just a set of old creatures. It is a lesson in how Pokemon turns absence into play.

entries.human_title: When ownership became the card's grammar

special_identification_instructions.summary: Gym Challenge identity is owner-plus-species. Agents should not flatten owner-named rows into ordinary Pokémon names.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: Identifying or comparing English Gym Challenge cards.

entries.why_it_matters: Gym Challenge is less about discovering new creatures than seeing old ones under someone else's hand. Blaine turns Charizard into a lesson in volatility, Misty makes Gyarados rebellious, Rocket makes Mewtwo and Zapdos feel captured, and the trainer portraits stare back from the checklist. The set matters because it makes relationship part of identity.

entries.human_title: The first English binder of borrowed teams

special_identification_instructions.summary: Gym Heroes is an English assembly of Gym-era materials; agents must keep owner name, row number, and Japanese/source-product lineage visible.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: Identifying or comparing English Gym Heroes cards.

entries.why_it_matters: Gym Heroes is where the English game learns that a Pokémon card can belong to someone. The creatures are familiar, but the ownership changes the air: Brock makes the rocks patient, Erika makes the grass gentle, Surge makes electricity disciplined, and Misty turns water into personality. It is the start of the owner-name grammar that Gym Challenge later sharpens.

entries.human_title: Jumbo cards - WoC-era bounded subset: oversized memory before it becomes a bucket

special_identification_instructions.summary: Confirm oversized Jumbo physical format and exact distribution route before treating a familiar card name or art lineage as this catalog row.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, binder photo, or agent search result names an English Jumbo, oversized, Top Deck, Warner Bros., or Best of Game Winner Jumbo card.

entries.why_it_matters: Jumbo is where the card stops pretending it belongs in a deck and starts acting like a poster, prize, magazine insert, or movie object. This bounded WotC-era slice is small on purpose: Top Deck Pikachu, the Warner Bros. triple birds, and the BattleZone / Best of Game Winner Jumbos are allowed to speak before the later Jumbo universe floods the room. The agent's job is to keep the physical format visible, because the art may look familiar while the object is doing a different job.

entries.human_title: The forest where the binder opens

special_identification_instructions.summary: English Jungle is a 64-row set where holo rares 1-16 have non-holo rare mirrors 17-32, and no-symbol claims belong to Unlimited Jungle holo rares only unless another sourced branch is provided.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Jungle, base2, no symbol, no set symbol, 1st Edition, Unlimited, holo, non-holo, Eeveelution, Scyther, Snorlax, Pikachu, Prerelease Clefable, W Promo Pikachu, gold-border Meowth, Base Set 2, or Legendary Collection.

entries.why_it_matters: Jungle is where the English game stops feeling like only a launch apparatus and starts feeling like a place. The first set taught the grammar; Jungle gives the binder a habitat: Eevee splitting into Flareon, Jolteon, and Vaporeon, Snorlax blocking the path, Scyther flashing through the grass, Pikachu tucked among commons, and a whole folklore of set-symbol and print errors waiting at the lower right. For the protocol, it is a beautiful troublemaker. Same name can mean holo or non-holo, ordinary or no-symbol, base2 or a later reprint. The card has to tell you which forest it came from.

special_identification_instructions.summary: Legendary Collection identity is reprint-plus-treatment: source lineage, set mark, foil state, and theme-deck exceptions all matter.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: Identifying or comparing Legendary Collection cards, especially reverse holos or theme-deck non-holos.

entries.why_it_matters: Legendary Collection is not a normal expansion so much as a memory machine. Wizards takes the early binder canon, gives it a new set mark, and then covers the card body in fireworks foil. The result is wonderfully strange: the same childhood images, but louder, shinier, and suddenly separate from their origin rows.

entries.human_title: The set where Neo chooses a side

special_identification_instructions.summary: Neo Destiny uses 105 printed checklist cards plus 113 modeled catalog rows; Shining rows need explicit row-number handling.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: Identifying or comparing Neo Destiny cards, especially Shining rows numbered 106 through 113.

entries.why_it_matters: Neo Destiny feels like the Neo era looking in a mirror. The Dark cards keep the Team Rocket shadow alive, the Light cards answer with care, and the Shining cards sit outside the normal checklist like hidden proof that rarity can become mythology. It is late Wizards-era Pokemon at its most theatrical: not just new monsters, but moral weather.

special_identification_instructions.summary: Neo Discovery's collector traps are mostly row-boundary traps: ruins lineage, paired holo/non-holo identities, and repeated species names must stay explicit.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, or agent search references Neo Discovery, Crossing the Ruins..., Espeon, Umbreon, Tyranitar, or a generic holo/non-holo Neo row.

entries.why_it_matters: Neo Discovery is where the second generation starts to feel ancient instead of merely new. Espeon and Umbreon make Eevee feel newly branching, Tyranitar gives Darkness a heavy body, and the Unown/Ruin Wall atmosphere turns the binder page into a little dig site. It is a set about finding out that Pokemon history has rooms behind it.

special_identification_instructions.summary: Neo Genesis is the Johto doorway, but agents must keep row number, baby/energy rules, and multi-row starter identities explicit.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, or binder import references Neo Genesis, Gold/Silver/New World, Lugia, Pichu, Metal Energy, or a Johto starter final evolution.

entries.why_it_matters: Neo Genesis is the sound of the Pokemon world opening another door. Lugia gives the era a mythic center, Pichu rewrites evolution backward, Metal Energy makes a new kind of durability legible, and the Johto starters arrive with competing power engines instead of simple nostalgia. It is not just more cards; it is the TCG learning how to be a sequel.

special_identification_instructions.summary: Neo Revelation's main trap is the 64 printed / 66 total Shining boundary plus repeated legendary names.

Then the Crystal Pokemon arrive beyond the printed count, changing type when energy touches them, as if the card itself is admitting it can be several things for one turn. It is late Wizards-era Pokemon at its strangest and most beautiful.

It is exactly the kind of set an agent should understand as culture, not just inventory.

Kangaskhan is almost too perfect here: a parent Pokemon with its child in the pouch, carrying the emotional thesis of the event. Touch Change! is the quieter marvel, a rules card that proves the tournament format itself became collectible. For an agent, the lesson is not just name matching. That is the assembly worth preserving. It is cartridge, manual, insert, Sugimori line, old-back holo desire, and a tiny printed mark all meeting in one card. The agent's job is to keep that contact legible without pretending the catalog has touched the seller's actual copy.

entries.human_title: The first game night in a box

special_identification_instructions.summary: Gift Pack is a product-component context, not a fixed deck-list proof. Preserve starter_a/starter_b lane identity, unresolved special-card slots, and unverified missing-symbol risk before using any row in transaction logic.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Gift Pack, ギフトパック, 122 cards, starter_a, starter_b, two starter decks, special cards, No Rarity, missing symbol, sealed Gift Pack, or launch Starter Pack.

entries.why_it_matters: Gift Pack is not exciting because it invents a new checklist. It is exciting because it shows Pokemon learning how to be played with another person. The product gathers two starter paths, a mat, counters, poison markers, instructions, and two unresolved special-card slots around the launch-card grammar. That makes it a little domestic, almost ceremonial: here are the cards, here is the table, here is enough apparatus for two people to learn the game together. For agents, the lesson is severe and useful: a product context can be historically rich while still not proving a fixed card list, a missing-symbol state, or a sealed unit's exact contents.

entries.human_title: Gold, Silver, to a New World... — when Johto becomes playable memory

special_identification_instructions.summary: Keep Gold, Silver, to a New World... as Japanese neo1 / 金、銀、新世界へ... with row-number identity; do not collapse it into English Neo Genesis or same-character rows.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Gold Silver New World, 金、銀、新世界へ, Neo Genesis, neo1, Lugia, Pichu, Johto starter, Metal Energy, or Darkness Energy.

entries.why_it_matters: Gold, Silver, to a New World... is the card-game doorway into Generation II: not just new names, but new ways for Pokemon to be young, metallic, dark, legendary, local, and mechanically different. It is one of the cleanest sets for teaching an agent that a card market is built from world grammar, not only famous characters.

entries.human_title: Misty as a deck, not just a character

special_identification_instructions.summary: Hanada City Gym cards can be missing rarity symbols because they are fixed-deck Japanese Gym cards; that must not be laundered into a 1996 No Rarity Base Set claim.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: Identifying or comparing Hanada City Gym / Misty cards, especially when a seller uses 'no rarity' language.

entries.why_it_matters: Hanada City Gym is where a Gym Leader becomes a small machine: 64 fixed cards, water lines, trainer personality, and a few rows that later look strange in English binders. This is exactly the kind of release an agent has to understand historically, because the same card-shaped object can mean fixed-deck memory in Japan, set rarity weirdness in English, and seller shorthand in a marketplace listing.

entries.human_title: The first forest before the mirrors

special_identification_instructions.summary: Japanese Pokemon Jungle is a 48-row Japanese booster release with rarity symbols and no English-style holo/non-holo duplicate numbering. Preserve Japanese row identity before comparing to English Jungle, Base Set 2, Legendary Collection, or no-symbol folklore.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Pokemon Jungle, ポケモンジャングル, PMCG2, Japanese Jungle, Jungle, no symbol, No Rarity, English Jungle, Base Set 2, Legendary Collection, holo, non-holo, Eeveelution, Scyther, Snorlax, or Pikachu.

entries.why_it_matters: Japanese Pokemon Jungle is the sequel before the sequel gets complicated. It has no English-style holo/non-holo mirror rows, no English no-symbol error folklore, and no need to inflate itself to 64 cards. It is a tighter object: 48 cards, a forest after the launch-room grammar, and a page where Eevee can split three ways while Snorlax blocks the path and Scyther cuts through the grass. For the catalog, this is the clean branch that teaches comparison: same forest memory, different assembly.

special_identification_instructions.summary: Preserve the Gym deck product boundary: 64-card product context, 25 unique catalog rows, missing-symbol deck lane, not Base No Rarity.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Kuchiba City Gym, Lt. Surge deck, クチバシティジム マチス, Vermilion City Gym, Lt. Surge's Pikachu, Lt. Surge's Raichu, missing rarity, no rarity, Sans rarete, Gym Heroes, or Gym Challenge.

entries.why_it_matters: Kuchiba City Gym is the Lt. Surge deck doing exactly what a Gym deck should do: turning a character into a working machine. The electricity is not abstract. It is his Pikachu twice, his Raichu, his Magneton, his Electrode, his Electabuzz, his gym, his secret mission, his treaty. That is why this release is useful for agents. A seller may say no rarity, Gym Heroes, Lt. Surge, or just Pikachu, but the real identity is a product route with a commander stamped across the cards.

special_identification_instructions.summary: Preserve Leaders' Stadium as a 96-row Japanese booster with rarity symbols, distinct from gym deck missing-symbol lanes and English Gym Heroes assembly.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Leaders' Stadium, Gym Heroes, Japanese Gym Expansion 1, owner Pokemon, Rocket's Scyther, Misty's Gyarados, Lt. Surge's Pikachu, The Rocket's Trap, or missing rarity.

entries.why_it_matters: Leaders' Stadium is where the Gym idea becomes too large for a deck box. Brock, Misty, Erika, Lt. Surge, and Rocket all step into one booster field, and suddenly Pokemon cards are not just creatures with attacks. They are loyalties, places, methods, traps, wishes, and gym rules. It feels like the game discovering that a card can carry social geography: who trained it, where it belongs, and what kind of room it wants the battle to happen in.

entries.human_title: Mysterious Mountains — when the e-Card frame becomes terrain

special_identification_instructions.summary: Keep Mysterious Mountains as Japanese E5 / 神秘なる山 with row-number and official-count boundary identity; do not collapse it into English Skyridge or same-character rows.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Mysterious Mountains, 神秘なる山, Skyridge, E5, e-Card, Charizard, Celebi, Moltres, Articuno, Gyarados, or Ancient Ruins.

entries.why_it_matters: Mysterious Mountains is late e-Card atmosphere: old powers climb into a scannable frame, ruins become rules, and the row map itself has edges worth preserving. It teaches agents that a set can be a landscape, not just a release date and a pile of names.

entries.human_title: The cave opens under the first year

special_identification_instructions.summary: Preserve the Japanese 48-row release boundary, rarity-symbol context, and local catalog row id before comparing to English Fossil or Base No Rarity.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Mystery of the Fossils, Japanese Fossil, 化石の秘密, PMCG3, Mew Fossil, Fossil Dragonite, or Mysterious Fossil.

entries.why_it_matters: Mystery of the Fossils is smaller than English Fossil and stranger in the hand. It feels like the Japanese release where early Pokemon turns from playground creatures toward buried machinery: fossil evolution, cave ghosts, legendary weather, and Mew as a mythic punctuation mark. The set is not only about old Pokemon. It is about the pleasure of finding a creature world under the one you thought you knew.

special_identification_instructions.summary: Preserve the gym-deck product boundary: 64-card product context, 25 unique catalog rows, missing-symbol deck lane, not Base No Rarity.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Nivi City Gym, Brock deck, ニビシティジム タケシ, Brock's Onix, Brock's Zubat, common rare, missing rarity, or No Rarity.

entries.why_it_matters: Nivi City Gym is where the binder stops treating Brock as a character and starts treating him as infrastructure. The creatures belong to him, the city belongs to him, even the training method belongs to him. It is wonderfully specific: a 1998 Japanese deck object that turns Gym Leader identity into play, then later leaves strange fossils of itself in English Gym Heroes common rares. The charm is not chase gloss. It is ownership becoming grammar.

entries.human_title: Pokemon Card VS — when ownership becomes encounter design

special_identification_instructions.summary: Keep Pokemon Card VS as Japanese VS1 / ポケモンカード★VS with trainer-owner and row-number identity; do not collapse owner rows into species-only searches.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Pokemon Card VS, ポケモンカード★VS, VS1, trainer-owned Pokemon, Karen, Lance, Rocket, Falkner, Bugsy, Jasmine, Clair, or any VS Technical Machine.

entries.why_it_matters: Pokemon Card VS turns the binder into a battle route. The card is no longer just Skarmory or Umbreon or Charizard; it is Falkner’s, Karen’s, Lance’s, Rocket’s. That owner label changes the desire, the memory, and the agent’s matching rules.

entries.human_title: Pokemon Card web — when old card memory goes through a new route

special_identification_instructions.summary: Keep Pokemon Card web as Japanese web1 / ポケモンカード★web with route and row-number identity; do not collapse it into old-set, promo, or famous-species rows.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Pokemon Card web, ポケモンカード★web, web1, e-Card, Dark Charizard, Dark Blastoise, Surfing Pikachu, legendary bird, or web release.

entries.why_it_matters: Pokemon Card web is a strange, compact bridge: the cards feel familiar, even nostalgic, but the route is new. That is exactly why agents need it. A famous name is not enough; the web apparatus, row number, and missing-row honesty are part of the object.

entries.human_title: The soundtrack becomes a card binder

special_identification_instructions.summary: Song Best Collection is a media-product reprint context; CD inclusion, earlier promotion, language, and variant lane must not be collapsed.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, or binder import says Song Best, CD promo, Japanese CD, unnumbered promo, or names one of the included cards without distribution context.

entries.why_it_matters: Pokemon Song Best Collection is one of those objects that makes the franchise feel assembled by many hands at once. It is a music CD, but tucked inside is a little card-memory cabinet: starters, mythics, Nintendo 64 campaign oddities, Computer Error, and even an English Pikachu. The joy is not that it behaves like a normal set. The joy is that it does not. It shows Pokemon becoming media infrastructure, where songs, promotions, campaigns, and cards all point back at the same growing world.

entries.human_title: The starter kit that taught the protocol its favorite warning

special_identification_instructions.summary: Quick Starter is a red/green deck-kit rollup and a missing-symbol trap lane; appearance never substitutes for provenance.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, or binder import says Quick Starter, Red Green Gift Set, QSGS, no rarity trainer, or names one of the five sensitive trainer rows.

entries.why_it_matters: Quick Starter Gift Set is almost a perfect little protocol parable. It was built to make play immediate: two decks, red and green, a ready-made way to sit down and battle. But for collectors it became something sharper, because some of its missing-symbol trainer reprints look close enough to Base No Rarity cards to tempt a sloppy story. That is why this product matters so much here. It teaches the agent that resemblance is not provenance, and that the assembly history of a card can matter more than the most obvious thing printed in the corner.

entries.human_title: The green half of the lesson

special_identification_instructions.summary: The Green Deck is a child lane inside Quick Starter; lane membership and missing-symbol caveats must remain visible.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, or binder import says Quick Starter Green Deck, QSGSG, green deck, no-rarity trainer, or one of the Green Deck row names.

entries.why_it_matters: The Green Deck is Quick Starter at its most welcoming: Bulbasaur at the door, little evolution lines, a few strange old Vending memories, then Mewtwo and Chansey waiting deeper in the lane. It feels gentle until the identification work starts. Then it becomes serious, because the same missing-symbol surface that makes these cards feel old can mislead an agent unless the green child lane stays attached to every row.

entries.human_title: The red half of the lesson

special_identification_instructions.summary: The Red Deck is a child lane inside Quick Starter Gift Set; preserve the lane, row order, and missing-symbol trap context.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Quick Starter Red Deck, red deck, QSGSR, Red Green Gift Set, no-rarity deck card, old-back Pikachu, old-back Squirtle, or missing-symbol trainer.

entries.why_it_matters: The Red Deck is Quick Starter with the lights on. It starts soft with Squirtle, then lets Pikachu appear twice, then lets Raichu and Zapdos make the deck feel charged. That is the fun part. The serious part is stranger: the same product that feels like a beginner bridge is also one of the best traps for a careless No Rarity search. A missing symbol can be visible and still point to the wrong assembly history.

entries.human_title: When the binder learns who owns the Pokemon

special_identification_instructions.summary: Rocket Gang is the 65-row Japanese release; keep it separate from English Team Rocket and from the later Team Rocket Gift Pack deck-component context.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, slab label, or agent search says Rocket Gang, Japanese Team Rocket, PMCG4, Dark Pokemon, Dark Charizard, or Team Rocket secret card.

entries.why_it_matters: Rocket Gang is the set where the card game lets the story darken without leaving the table. The Pokemon are still Kanto bodies a collector recognizes, but the frame changes the relationship: these are creatures seen through Team Rocket's hands. That is why the set feels bigger than a villain logo. It teaches the catalog to track ownership, mood, numbering, and release language before trusting the familiar silhouette.

entries.human_title: Split Earth — when fracture becomes collection grammar

special_identification_instructions.summary: Keep Split Earth as Japanese E4 / 裂けた大地 with duplicate-name and row-map identity; do not collapse it into English Aquapolis or same-character rows.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Split Earth, 裂けた大地, Aquapolis, E4, Umbreon, Ho-Oh, underground, crystal shard, or late-number row.

entries.why_it_matters: Split Earth makes the e-Card landscape feel unstable in the best way: underground routes, fossil returns, duplicated Umbreon desire, artifact cards, and a Ho-Oh at the map edge. It is a set where the agent must learn that terrain, number, and row boundary are part of the story.

special_identification_instructions.summary: Series 1 Starter Pack is a possible-content context, not a fixed sealed-deck proof. Preserve the 102-row possible-content model, the 60-card product context, and mixed No Rarity risk before using any row in transaction logic.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Series 1 Starter Pack, 第1弾スターターパック, Starter Deck, deck pull, No Rarity, missing symbol, sealed deck, 60-card deck, Expansion Pack, Gift Pack, Base Set, trainer text, or Basic Energy.

entries.why_it_matters: The Series 1 Starter Pack is where the first Japanese card pool becomes an invitation instead of only a checklist. It gathers Pokemon, trainers, and energy into the idea of a 60-card deck, but the catalog has to speak carefully: this is a possible-content pool, not a prophecy about a sealed deck. That tension is the whole charm. The product is close to the birth of No Rarity, close to Expansion Pack, close to Gift Pack, and close to the first kitchen-table lesson. It teaches the agent that launch history is not one lane. It is pack, deck, energy floor, random contents, and the human desire to actually play.

special_identification_instructions.summary: Preserve the Gym deck product boundary: 64-card product context, 28 unique catalog rows, missing-symbol deck lane, not Base No Rarity.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Tamamushi City Gym, Erika deck, タマムシシティジム エリカ, Celadon City Gym, Erika's Oddish, Erika's Vileplume, Erika's Dratini, no rarity, missing rarity, Sans rarete, Gym Heroes, Gym Challenge, or Erika Theme Deck.

entries.why_it_matters: Tamamushi City Gym is not just a Grass deck. It is Erika as a cultivated system: Oddish and Bellsprout lines, Vileplume and Victreebel at the top, Dratini as a soft surprise, then maids, perfume, charity, manners, city, and resources. The cards feel gentle, but the catalog work is strict. A seller can say no rarity, Erika, Celadon, or Gym Heroes; the agent has to keep the Japanese deck lane intact.

entries.human_title: The Rocket apparatus in a box

special_identification_instructions.summary: Team Rocket Gift Pack is a product context with two documented 60-card decks, but this catalog has unresolved fixed deck lists and only models candidate rows.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, sealed product note, or agent search says Team Rocket Gift Pack, Rocket Gang Gift Pack, two Rocket decks, fixed Rocket deck, or Gift Pack Dark Charizard.

entries.why_it_matters: Team Rocket Gift Pack is where Rocket Gang stops being only a booster world and becomes a table for two. The counters, poison markers, playmat, guidebook, and two fixed decks matter because they show Pokemon being packaged as a ritual of play, not just as cards to pull. The catalog has to be unusually honest here: the product is real, the 120-card shape is sourced, but the exact fixed deck lists are not pinned in this dataset yet.

entries.human_title: Town on No Map — when coordinates become the collector problem

special_identification_instructions.summary: Keep Town on No Map as Japanese E2 / 地図にない町 with paired-name row identity; do not collapse rare/holo pairs or English Aquapolis rows.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Town on No Map, 地図にない町, Aquapolis, E2, Zapdos, Espeon, Umbreon, Pokemon Park, Power Plant, or paired rows.

entries.why_it_matters: Town on No Map is an e-Card place that refuses to be flattened. The title is almost a warning to the agent: if the town is not on a map, the row number is the map. Zapdos, Espeon, and Umbreon each split into paired desire, while civic cards make the release feel inhabited.

entries.human_title: Wind from the Sea — when the shore gets coordinates

special_identification_instructions.summary: Keep Wind from the Sea as Japanese E3 / 海からの風 with duplicate-name and late-number row identity; do not collapse rare/holo pairs, secret rows, or English Aquapolis rows.
special_identification_instructions.trigger: A listing, want, scan, or agent memory says Wind from the Sea, 海からの風, Aquapolis, E3, Lugia, Kingdra, Entei, Tyranitar, Scizor, Steelix, or late-number secret rows.

entries.why_it_matters: Wind from the Sea feels like the e-Card coast learning to keep records. The set title gives the emotional weather, but the cards teach discipline: Vileplume can be rare or holo, Kingdra can be holo or secret, Lugia can sit at the edge like a wave you only notice if the number is still visible. It is beautiful because it is breezy and strict at once.
